name: Kannayiranathar Temple, Tirukkannarkoil
deity: Shiva as Kannayiranathar (Kannayiram Udayar), with the goddess Murugu Valar Kothai Nayaki (Kothai Nayaki)
period: Tevaram era (hymned 7th century); later Chola structural temple
summary: Kurumanakkudi, also called Tirukkannarkoil or Kannarkovil, near Vaitheeswaran Koil in the Mayiladuthurai country, honours Shiva as Kannayiranathar — Kannayiram Udayar — with the goddess Murugu Valar Kothai Nayaki. A Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar, it is a quiet shrine of the northern Kaveri delta.

sections.history: Kurumanakkudi — Tirukkannarkoil, also Kannarkovil — lies about 5 km from Vaitheeswaran Koil and 8 km from Sirkazhi, in Tarangambadi taluk of Mayiladuthurai district. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, hymned in the Tevaram by Tirugnana Sambandar, counted among the Shiva shrines on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The stone temple is of the Chola period and later. (Older listings give the district as Nagapattinam, from which Mayiladuthurai was later carved out.)
sections.architecture: A Dravidian delta temple, the shrine enshrines Kannayiranathar — Kannayiram Udayar — in the sanctum, with the goddess Murugu Valar Kothai Nayaki (also Kothai Nayaki, Sugandha Kundalambikai) in her own shrine, a Nandi and the parivara devatas about the prakara. The walled courtyard and modest gopuram are typical of the Shiva temples of the northern delta near Sirkazhi.
sections.legends: Shiva is worshipped here as Kannayiranathar — Kannayiram Udayar, 'the lord of the thousand eyes' — a name that echoes the story of Indra of the thousand eyes, who by tradition worshipped at the delta shrines. The goddess is praised as Murugu Valar Kothai Nayaki, 'she whose garland breathes fragrance,' and as Sugandha Kundalambikai. As with many smaller delta shrines, the fuller sthala purana survives chiefly in local tradition and Sambandar's verses.
sections.festivals: The temple observes Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March), Navaratri in Purattasi (September–October) and the Mondays of Karthikai, with Pradosha worship, at the quiet scale of a village shrine. Pilgrims on the Vaitheeswaran Koil–Sirkazhi stretch of the northern Kaveri include Tirukkannarkoil among their stops.
sections.experience: At Tirukkannarkoil the pilgrim comes to a quiet shrine of the thousand-eyed lord. Before Kannayiranathar and Murugu Valar Kothai Nayaki, in the green country near Vaitheeswaran Koil, the visitor finds the unhurried grace of a Tevaram temple of the northern Kaveri delta.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Kurumanakkudi (Tirukkannarkoil) lies about 5 km from Vaitheeswaran Koil and 8 km from Sirkazhi, in Tarangambadi taluk of Mayiladuthurai district; a signposted branch road off the Vaitheeswarankoil–Mayiladuthurai route leads to it. Vaitheeswaran Koil and Sirkazhi are the nearest rail heads, with buses and taxis to the village.
